title: Choosing the best summary
blurb: Pick the summary that covers every paragraph, in order, with the right emphasis and nothing added.
question: A four-paragraph HESI A2 passage describes a problem, a hospital's solution and the results, and the question asks 'Which is the best summary of the passage?' One choice retells the first paragraph in detail; another covers every paragraph briefly but ends with 'every hospital should do this.' Which is the best summary, if either?

teach.body: Formally, a summary is a brief restatement, in your own words, of a text's main idea and its most important supporting points, in the same order and with the same emphasis as the original. It is objective: no opinions, no new information, no minor details. In plain English: if a friend asked 'What did that article say?', a summary is the honest 20-second answer that covers the whole thing.

teach.caption: Both restate in new words. Only a summary condenses.

head: Keep in a summary
Leave out of a summary
rows: The key point of every paragraph

teach.body:
(1) Hospitals can be surprisingly noisy at night. Monitors beep, carts rattle down hallways, and staff talk at the nurses' station a few feet from patients' doors. Sound levels on some units at 2 a.m. rival those of a busy office.

(2) That noise matters. Patients who are woken again and again often report feeling more tired and anxious the next day, and in surveys many name poor sleep as the worst part of their stay. Rest is also when the body does much of its repair work.

(3) Some hospitals have responded with 'quiet hours' from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. Lights in hallways are dimmed, alarm volumes are lowered where it is safe, and nonurgent tasks such as restocking are moved to daytime. Staff hold conversations away from patient rooms.

(4) Where quiet hours have been tried, patients report sleeping better. The changes cost little, but they depend on every shift following them.

items: Label each paragraph in a phrase: (1) hospitals are noisy at night; (2) noise harms patients' rest; (3) quiet hours cut the noise; (4) patients sleep better.
Find the thread that ties them together: night noise is a problem that quiet hours can reduce.
Write the labels in the same order, in your own words: 'Night noise in hospitals disrupts patients' sleep, and low-cost quiet hours that dim lights and lower noise help them sleep better.'

Check: every paragraph covered? Nothing added? No minor detail (the 2 a.m. comparison, the exact hours) taking center stage? On the HESI A2, with about 65 seconds per item, test the four options against your labels rather than rereading the passage.

steps.label: Summary
steps.sub: Noise is a problem; quiet hours reduce it

teach.text: HESI-style 'best summary' items lean on four wrong summaries: one that covers only the first (or last) paragraph, one built on a memorable statistic, one that slips in an opinion or recommendation ('so every hospital should...'), and one that reverses the emphasis by making a minor point the center. A summary can be accurate sentence by sentence and still be wrong because it is incomplete.

teach.body: Jamal Reed, applying to a BSN program, sees four summaries of the noise passage. 'Alarms, carts and staff conversations make hospitals noisy at night' covers paragraph 1 only. 'Quiet hours run from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.' is a minor detail. 'Noise harms sleep, so all hospitals must adopt quiet hours' adds a recommendation. 'Night noise disrupts patients' sleep, and quiet hours help them rest' covers all four paragraphs with nothing added. Jamal picks the last one.

items: A summary is short, in your own words, and covers the main idea plus every paragraph's key point.
Keep the original order and emphasis; stay objective.
Leave out opinions, new information, minor details and nonessential quotations.
A paraphrase is about the same length as the part it restates; a summary condenses.
Method: label each paragraph, find the thread, then check for gaps and additions.

summary: You can now summarize a multi-paragraph text by labeling each paragraph and finding the thread that connects them. You can also reject summaries that are incomplete, built on a minor detail, reversed in emphasis or tinted with opinion.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Honeybees cannot see the color red, but they can see ultraviolet light, which humans cannot. Many flowers have ultraviolet patterns on their petals that work like landing strips, guiding bees toward the nectar at the center.

These hidden patterns help the flowers too. As a bee crawls toward the nectar, pollen sticks to its body, and the bee carries it to the next flower it visits. A signal invisible to people helps the insect find food and the plant reproduce.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
options: Bees see ultraviolet light but not red, and many flowers have ultraviolet petal patterns that work like landing strips to guide the bees to nectar.
Ultraviolet patterns on flowers guide bees to nectar and help the bees spread pollen, so gardeners should choose flowers that have these patterns.
Flowers show bees ultraviolet patterns people cannot see, leading them to nectar, and the bees then carry pollen that helps the plants reproduce.
Bees use ultraviolet light to reproduce, and flowers guide the bees toward their pollen by showing them patterns in shades of red on their petals.
A.why: The best summary covers both paragraphs in order: the patterns guide bees to nectar (paragraph 1), and the bees then carry pollen that helps the plant reproduce (paragraph 2). It adds nothing.

whyNot.0: Accurate but incomplete: it covers paragraph 1 only and leaves out the benefit to the flowers.
whyNot.1: It adds a recommendation for gardeners that the passage never makes, so it is not objective.
whyNot.3: Distortion: the plants reproduce, not the bees, and the passage says bees cannot see red.

A.q: Which statement correctly describes how a summary differs from a paraphrase?
options: A summary keeps the author's exact words; a paraphrase restates them in new words.
A summary adds the reader's view of the text; a paraphrase stays strictly objective.
A summary restates one paragraph; a paraphrase condenses the whole passage at once.
A summary condenses the key points; a paraphrase is about as long as the original.
A.why: Both are written in your own words, but a summary is much shorter and keeps only the main idea and key points, while a paraphrase restates a specific part at about the same length.

whyNot.0: A summary is also in your own words; quoting is not what makes it a summary.
whyNot.1: A summary must be objective too: no opinions.
whyNot.2: This reverses the two: a summary covers the whole text, and a paraphrase restates a specific part.

A.q: A student's summary of a three-paragraph article on a city's new recycling rules reads: 'The city now collects glass separately, has added a second weekly pickup, and fines businesses that do not sort waste, which is a smart and overdue change.' What is the main problem with this summary?
options: It adds a judgment that the article does not make.
It is nearly the same length as the paragraphs it restates.
It reports the article's points in a different order.
It quotes the article's wording instead of restating it.
A.why: 'Which is a smart and overdue change' is the student's opinion. A summary must be objective and add nothing that the text does not say.

whyNot.1: The summary is one sentence covering three paragraphs, so it has condensed the text.
whyNot.2: Nothing in the stem shows the points are out of order; the clear fault is the added judgment.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests it copies the article's wording; the fault is the opinion at the end.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Many rural counties have no clinic of their own. Residents may drive an hour or more to see a doctor or nurse, and some skip care altogether.

To close that gap, several states now train community health workers: local residents who visit patients at home, help them keep track of medications and schedule appointments.

In one county, emergency room visits dropped in the program's first two years. Workers say patients trust them because they are neighbors, not strangers.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
options: Emergency room visits in one rural county dropped during the two years after trained health workers began visiting patients in their homes.
Where rural clinics are scarce, trained local residents now visit patients at home to support their care, and early results suggest it helps.
Rural counties often have no clinic, so residents must drive an hour or more to reach a doctor or nurse, and some of them skip care altogether.
States have improved rural health care everywhere by training local residents to replace the clinic staff who used to treat their neighbors.
B.why: This covers all three paragraphs in order: the problem (few clinics), the response (trained local health workers visiting homes) and the early results.

whyNot.0: Too narrow: it is built on one statistic from paragraph 3 and skips the problem and the program itself.
whyNot.3: Distortion and overstatement: the workers support care where clinics are missing; they do not replace clinic staff, and results come from one county.

B.q:
Read the passage.

Riverside Middle School started a 'walking school bus' in September. Parent volunteers walk set routes each morning, picking up children at marked stops.

The program started slowly. Only about 30 students joined in the first month, and rain canceled six walks, so organizers bought rain ponchos and added a second route in October.

By spring, more than 200 students walked each day. The principal says morning traffic outside the school has eased, and teachers report that walkers arrive alert.

Which sentence would be LEAST appropriate to include in a summary of the passage?
options: Riverside began a morning walking program led by parent volunteers.
The program grew from about 30 students to more than 200 by spring.
Organizers bought rain ponchos after six walks had been canceled.
The program has eased traffic and helped students arrive alert.
B.why: The ponchos are a minor detail inside paragraph 2. A summary keeps the main idea and key points, and the slow start can be captured in the growth figure without the poncho detail.

whyNot.0: This states the program itself, the core of paragraph 1.
whyNot.1: This captures the program's growth, the key point linking paragraphs 2 and 3.
whyNot.3: This states the results, the key point of paragraph 3.

B.q:
Read the passage.

The city of Dunmore will plant 5,000 trees over the next three years to cool neighborhoods that have little shade. Studies of local streets found that blocks without trees were several degrees hotter on summer afternoons.

The trees were chosen because they tolerate heat and drought, and planting will begin in the neighborhoods with the fewest trees.

One council member objected to the cost of watering young trees, but the plan passed by a vote of 7 to 2.

A student wrote this summary: 'A council member objected to the cost of watering new trees, but the city council still passed the plan by a vote of 7 to 2.' What is the main weakness of this summary?
options: It turns a minor point into the passage's central point.
It adds a personal opinion about the city council's vote.
It is nearly the same length as the paragraphs it restates.
It reports the vote in a way that contradicts the passage.
B.why: The passage is mainly about planting trees to cool neighborhoods with little shade. The objection and the vote are a minor final point, so making them the whole summary reverses the emphasis.

whyNot.1: The student's sentence reports facts from the passage without giving a personal opinion.
whyNot.2: The summary is a single sentence, far shorter than the passage.
whyNot.3: The vote of 7 to 2 matches the passage; the problem is what the summary leaves out.

C.q:
Read the passage.

At Grandview Hospital, nurses used to exchange information about patients at the nurses' station during shift change. Details sometimes got lost, and patients had no chance to correct mistakes.

Two years ago, the hospital moved these handoffs to the bedside. The outgoing and incoming nurses now meet in each room, review the chart together and invite the patient to add anything missing.

The change was not easy. Handoffs took longer at first, and some nurses worried about discussing private information in shared rooms. After the hospital added a short script and privacy guidelines, handoff times returned to normal, and patient surveys showed that people felt better informed.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
options: Because nurses lost details at the station, Grandview now has patients read their own charts aloud at shift change while the nurses listen.
Grandview moved handoffs to the bedside to include patients; early delays and privacy worries were solved, and patients felt better informed.
Bedside handoffs at Grandview took longer at first and worried nurses about privacy, which shows the hospital's change has been a mistake.
Grandview moved its shift handoffs to the bedside, and every hospital should copy it, because its patients now report feeling better informed.
C.why: It covers each paragraph in order (the old problem, the bedside change, the difficulties and how they were solved) and adds no opinion.

whyNot.0: Distortion: nurses review the chart together and invite the patient to add details; patients do not read their own charts aloud.
whyNot.2: Opposite of the passage: the problems were solved, and the conclusion that it was a mistake is the student's own judgment.
whyNot.3: It adds a recommendation for every hospital that the passage never makes.

C.q:
Read the passage.

For years, Fairview Public Library charged late fines of 25 cents a day. Staff noticed that many families with unpaid fines stopped visiting, even after returning their books.

In 2023, the library ended late fines. Patrons still pay for lost items, and borrowing is paused when a book is more than a month overdue.

Within a year, the number of active cardholders rose by 18 percent, and most overdue books still came back. The director says the small loss in fine income was worth bringing families back.

Which sentence best completes this summary? 'Fairview Public Library ended late fines because they were keeping families away, though it still charges for lost items. ____'
options: The fines had been 25 cents a day until the library dropped them in 2023.
Other libraries should drop fines, since families matter more than money.
Since then, fewer books have come back, but more families have joined.
Since then, more people use the library, and most books still come back.
C.why: The summary already covers paragraphs 1 and 2. The missing piece is paragraph 3's result: more active cardholders, with most books still returned.

whyNot.0: This repeats a minor detail from paragraph 1 and leaves the results out entirely.
whyNot.1: This adds a recommendation and an opinion that the passage does not state.
whyNot.2: Distortion: the passage says most overdue books still came back.

C.q:
Read the passage.

When Marisol's grandfather was told he had high blood pressure, she noticed that his kitchen shelves were lined with canned soups.

Like many people, he rarely added salt at the table, so he assumed his diet was low in sodium. In fact, most of the sodium in a typical American diet comes from packaged and restaurant foods, not from the salt shaker.

Reading nutrition labels, choosing lower-sodium versions of favorite foods and cooking more meals at home can all help people cut back.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
options: Most dietary sodium comes from packaged and restaurant foods, not the salt shaker, so labels and home cooking can help people cut back.
Marisol noticed that her grandfather, who had just been told he has high blood pressure, kept many canned soups on his kitchen shelves.
People can lower their sodium intake by reading nutrition labels, choosing lower-sodium foods and cooking more of their own meals at home.
Canned soups cause high blood pressure, so people who want to stay healthy should stop eating packaged and restaurant foods altogether.
C.why: Paragraph 1 is an anecdote that introduces the topic. The key points are paragraph 2 (where sodium really comes from) and paragraph 3 (how to cut back). This option covers both.

whyNot.1: Too narrow: it retells the opening anecdote, which only introduces the topic.
whyNot.2: Incomplete: it covers paragraph 3 but drops paragraph 2's central point about where sodium comes from.
whyNot.3: Overstatement: the passage never says canned soup causes high blood pressure or that people should stop eating packaged food.

reteach.title: Recapping a movie for a friend
reteach.question: A friend missed a movie you saw and asks what happened. How would you answer in thirty seconds, and how is that like a HESI A2 summary?

blocks.body: You would not describe only the opening scene (incomplete), list every line of dialogue (too detailed) or spend your time on the snack bar (minor detail). You also would not mix in your review, 'it was boring', if they only asked what happened (opinion). You would give the beginning, middle and end in order, in your own words. That is exactly what a good summary of a three-paragraph passage does.

blocks.text: An accurate sentence can still be a bad summary. If it covers one paragraph, it fails, however true it is.

explain.body: A summary is brief, in your own words, and covers the main idea plus the key point of every paragraph, in the original order and emphasis. It is objective.

test.q: Which feature is required of a good summary of a multi-paragraph passage?
options: It includes at least one direct quotation from each paragraph.
It explains whether the reader agrees with the author's view.
It focuses on the most surprising statistic in the passage.
It restates the key point of each paragraph in the same order.
test.why: A summary must cover the whole text, keeping the original order and emphasis.

whyNot.0: Quotations are left out of a summary unless they are essential.
whyNot.1: A summary is objective; the reader's agreement is opinion.
whyNot.2: A single statistic is a supporting detail; centering it makes the summary too narrow.

explain.body: Both restate ideas in new words. A paraphrase restates one specific part at about the same length; a summary condenses the whole text to its key points.

explain.h: Typical length compared with the original

test.q: A student rewrites one 80-word paragraph from an article in her own words, keeping every detail, and ends up with 75 words. What has she written?
options: A summary
A paraphrase
A quotation
An inference
test.why: Restating one specific part in new words at about the same length, with every detail kept, is a paraphrase.

whyNot.0: A summary would condense the whole article to its key points, not keep every detail of one paragraph.
whyNot.2: A quotation uses the author's exact words; she used her own.
whyNot.3: An inference is a conclusion drawn from evidence; she only restated what the paragraph says.

explain.body: Give each paragraph a short label, then find the thread connecting the labels. The best summary is that thread plus the labels, in order.

test.q: A student labels the three paragraphs of a passage: (1) teens often sleep too little on school nights; (2) one district moved its high school start time from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m.; (3) attendance and grades rose afterward. Which summary best links these labels?
options: After one district moved its high school start time from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m., its attendance and grades rose.
Teens often sleep too little; a district that started high school later saw attendance and grades rise.
Teens often get too little sleep on school nights because their high schools begin classes before 8:30 a.m.
Every school district should start high school at 8:30 a.m. so that teens can sleep more on school nights.
test.why: It covers all three labels in order: the problem, the change and the result.

whyNot.0: It drops paragraph 1, the problem the change was meant to solve.
whyNot.2: It covers paragraph 1 only and adds a cause that the labels do not state.
whyNot.3: It adds a recommendation for every district that the passage does not make.

explain.body: Cut opinions and recommendations, information not in the text, minor details and side examples, and quotations that are not essential. Keep the emphasis the author gave each point.

test.q: A passage explains how a clinic shortened its waiting times by adding an online check-in system and an extra nurse on Mondays. Which sentence should be left out of a summary of it?
options: The clinic shortened its waiting times with two practical changes.
Patients can now check in online before arriving at the clinic.
An extra nurse now works at the clinic every Monday.
The new system is far better than the clinic's old paper forms.
test.why: 'Far better' is a judgment. Unless the author states it, an opinion has no place in an objective summary.

whyNot.0: This is the main idea of the passage.
whyNot.1: This is one of the two key changes the passage describes.
whyNot.2: This is the second key change the passage describes.
